chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim narrated from his father, from al-Hasan ibn al-Husayn, from Safwan, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, who said:

I bought a load (of goods) and gave part of its price, and left it with its owner. Then I was detained for a few days. Then I came to the seller of the load to take it, and he said, 'I have sold it.' So I laughed, then I said, 'By Allah, I will not leave you unless I litigate with you.' He said to me, 'Will you be satisfied with Abu Bakr ibn Ayash [as judge]?' I said, 'Yes.' So we went to him and narrated our story to him. Abu Bakr said, 'Whose opinion do you prefer that I judge between you two by: your companion's [the seller's] or someone else's?' I said, 'By my companion's [the seller's] opinion.'
I heard him [the Prophet, peace be upon him] say: 'Whoever buys something, let him bring the price within three days; otherwise, there is no sale for him [the buyer has the option to cancel].'

key_terms.أَبُو بَكْرٍ بْنِ عَيَّاش: A prominent judge (qadi) of the early Islamic period
key_terms.أُقَاضِيَكَ: I will litigate with you / take you to court
key_terms.اُحْتُبِسْتُ: I was detained or held up
key_terms.فَلاَ بَيْعَ لَهُ: There is no sale for him (the sale is not binding/voidable)
key_terms.مَحْمِل: A load or consignment of goods

ai.seo_question: What is the buyer's right to cancel a sale if they haven't paid the full price within three days?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the specific application of *khiyar al-majlis* (option of delay) in partial payment sales, establishing a three-day window for the buyer to complete the transaction. Abu Bakr ibn Ayash’s ruling, derived from the Prophet’s tradition, emphasizes that the sale remains revocable by the buyer if the full price is not tendered within this period, a principle highly valued in Shia jurisprudence for protecting buyers from seller default. This narrative underscores the importance of clear contractual terms and the prophetic precedent in resolving commercial disputes.
